passage: Tushar, twenty-five, got off the bus in a small hill town at dusk with his friend Yamini. His phone had died on the way, and the homestay was somewhere "near the old church". A man at the bus stand offered to walk them there for a fee and reached for Yamini's bag. Tushar gently took it back and kept it on his own shoulder. "We'll manage, thanks." He asked a woman at the fruit stall; she pointed uphill, past the post office. He asked a schoolboy, who said the same. Then a shopkeeper said downhill. Two against one. They went uphill, and at the post office, asked again. The church bell was right there. So was their homestay sign.

passage: On her first week in Kolkata for a new job, Vidya, twenty-four, needed to reach an office in Salt Lake from Howrah station. Her phone battery was at five percent. She asked a policeman, who told her the bus number. She asked a woman waiting at the stop, who said the same bus and added, "Get off at the water tank." Inside the bus, she asked the conductor to tell her the stop. Her colleague Yusuf, who met her at the office, laughed. "You found it faster than I did in my first week."

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Aditi, nine, found an old torch in the drawer. It didn't work. She sat on the balcony floor and unscrewed the top. A spring jumped out. Then a tiny bulb. Her uncle, Kiran chacha, came out with his toolbox. "Want to see how the switch works?" He handed her a small screwdriver and showed her how to hold it. Together they cleaned a rusty metal strip. The torch lit up. Aditi squealed.

I was sad for about ten minutes. Then Ammi's brother, who fixes bicycles, gave me a small screwdriver set and said I could use it only at his shop, with him beside me. Every Saturday after that I took something apart there. I still remember the feeling of that first coiled spring.

passage: I'm Disha, and the ceiling fan in our living room taught me more than any physics class. I was fourteen when it started wobbling and making a clicking sound. My father, Siddharth, said, "Come, hold the ladder, and watch." First he switched off the fan at the main switch. "Always first," he said. Then he climbed up, and I held the ladder steady. He showed me the loose screws on the blade holder, explained that the wobble came from one blade being heavier. He tightened them, and let me hand him each tool, telling me why he chose it. When the fan turned smoothly again, he said, "Your turn next time." That feeling of being able to fix things never left me.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do first before climbing up?
qa.a: He switched off the fan at the main switch.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the fan turned smoothly again?
qa.a: Disha felt proud and capable, a feeling that never left.

Dear Diary, Saturday.
Nani's sewing machine was stuck, so Zeenat Nani called me over. "Come, you have young eyes." She showed me where the thread was jammed under the plate, and made me unscrew two tiny screws. She told me why the thread knots: when it's pulled too tight. We cleaned out old fluff with a paintbrush and put a drop of oil where she pointed. She kept telling me stories about stitching my mother's school uniforms on this very machine. When it started humming again, Nani clapped. I felt so capable. Tomorrow she's teaching me how to thread it properly.
Vinita

passage: The tap in the second-floor hostel bathroom had leaked for a week. Thomas, twenty, watched a repair video on his phone, borrowed a spanner from the security guard and, after closing the valve under the sink, replaced the worn washer. When the dripping stopped, he felt ridiculously proud and sent a photo to the group. Two days later, a pipe under the common-room sink burst, spraying water across the floor. Thomas pulled up another video. It involved cutting and joining pipes. He looked at it for a long moment, then went to Charu ma'am, the warden. "This one's beyond me. I think you need a plumber." She nodded. "Good. Knowing that is part of fixing things."

passage:
Dear Vishal,

Remember I told you I'd fix my cracked phone screen myself with that repair video? Update: I didn't.

I ordered the screen, the tiny screwdrivers and the suction cup. I watched the video five times. It all looked so easy. But when I heated the edge and pried it open, a thin cable tore. Now the new screen works, but the camera doesn't. I spent an hour staring at it, feeling like an idiot.

Last month I fixed the wobbly table from a video and felt like a genius. I think I forgot that phones are not tables.

Next time, the repair shop.

Lokesh

qa.q: What stopped working after the repair?
qa.a: The camera doesn't work.

passage: You want to hear about my DIY phase? I'm Nilesh. At nineteen, I found repair videos and thought I could fix anything. First, my cycle brakes. Worked perfectly. I was so proud I told everyone. Then the leaking bathroom pipe in our flat. The video said, "Just tighten the joint." I tightened it too much and it cracked. Water everywhere. My flatmate Deepak and I spent the night mopping and calling the landlord. The plumber came next morning and said, "Brakes are one thing. Pipes under pressure are another." I felt so dismayed. Now, before any video repair, I ask: if this goes wrong, what's the worst that happens? If the answer is flood or fire, I call someone.

passage: Yuki, twenty-five, had replaced a light switch once in her flat in Osaka, following the instructions carefully. It had worked. So when the kitchen socket started sparking, she decided to fix it herself. She unscrewed the cover without turning off the power at the breaker. "It's just one wire," she thought. The screwdriver touched metal. There was a loud crack and a flash; she was thrown back, her hand numb. Her neighbour Clara heard the sound and ran in, switched off the breaker and called a doctor. Yuki's hand recovered in a few days. Afterwards, she called a licensed electrician. "One switch doesn't make me an electrician," she said quietly.

"It's fine, I'll be quick." Then his screwdriver slipped, and a spark jumped with a sharp crack. He jerked back, shaken, fingers tingling. Hafsa switched off the mains and phoned the office manager. The building's licensed electrician came that afternoon and found a faulty thermostat. Tushar didn't say much for the rest of the day.

passage:
Dear Francis,

I need to tell you about Saturday, because you'll hear it from the neighbours anyway.

The gas stove's knob was loose, and I've tightened it before, so I decided to fix the pipe connection behind it too. I didn't turn off the cylinder. I thought it would take two minutes. The moment I loosened the joint, I smelled a strong rush of gas. I panicked, turned the cylinder off, opened every window and ran out. The neighbours called the gas agency. The technician said I was lucky no one had lit anything.

I was so sure because the knob had been easy. From now on, gas and wiring go to licensed people.

Preeti

qa.q: What did Preeti not turn off before loosening the joint?
qa.a: The cylinder.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when the gas rushed out?
qa.a: Preeti panicked, suddenly frightened after being so sure.

qa.q: What lesson does Preeti draw, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Gas and wiring go to licensed people, because a small success with a knob doesn't make a gas pipe safe to fix.

qa.q: How might Francis feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Francis might feel shocked and worried, but relieved that Preeti is safe and has decided to use professionals.

grounding: A letter shows an adult overconfident from a small repair working on a gas pipe without shutting the supply, and deciding to use licensed people.

His neighbour Farida, who ran a hardware shop, was watching from the gate. She walked over. "Can you show him what's wrong with the motor?" The mechanic hesitated, then pointed vaguely. Farida suggested, "Let's get a second opinion." The next mechanic found a burnt capacitor and fixed it in half an hour. Joseph felt both relieved and a little foolish.

I want to record how Nandini, our newest trainer, runs her corner. Every sewing machine on her side has a small card listing the last oiling date. Her tools are hung on a board, each in its outline, so a missing pair of scissors is obvious at once. When a student tried to cut thick canvas with fabric scissors, Nandini stopped her gently and handed her the heavy shears. "Wrong tool, wrong result." In three months, not one of her machines has needed the repairman. The other side has called him four times. I have asked Nandini to show the other trainers her board on Monday.
Gargi

passage: Tejas, ten, lived in a flat in Chennai and got pocket money every Monday. Every Monday afternoon, he spent it at the shop below: chips, a cola, sticker packets. It felt wonderful for about ten minutes. Then his friend Samir came over with a new cricket bat he had saved up for over two months. Tejas held it and felt a pang of envy. "I want one." His mother said, "What if you kept a little each week in this jar?" She drew a picture of a bat on the jar. The next Monday, Tejas stood outside the shop, jingling coins, torn. He bought one packet of chips and put the rest in the jar. It felt strange, and a bit proud.

qa.q: How long had Samir saved for the bat?
qa.a: Over two months.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he held Samir's bat?
qa.a: He felt a pang of envy and a new wish for something bigger.

qa.q: What did Tejas's mother do that could help him?
qa.a: She gave him a jar with a picture of a bat on it, so the bigger wish stayed in front of him.

qa.q: How might Samir feel about his bat?
qa.a: Samir likely feels proud, having waited two months to buy it.

grounding: Shows a child who spends pocket money at once, then feels the pull of a bigger wish after seeing a friend's saved-for bat.

Tanvir: "All of it?"

Tanvir: "And the art set you showed me in the shop window?"
Aditi: (quiet) "I still want it. It's so much money."
Tanvir: "How does it feel, not having it?"
Aditi: "Bad. The ice cream is gone, but I still want the art set."
Tanvir: "What if we cut out a picture of the art set and stick it on your money box?"
Aditi: "So I remember when I want ice cream?"
Tanvir: "Exactly. You decide each week how much goes in."
Aditi: "Can I still have ice cream sometimes?"
Tanvir: "Sometimes. You choose."

qa.a: A picture of the art set on the money box, so Aditi remembers the bigger wish when choosing, while still deciding for herself.

passage:
Dear Irawati,

You asked how the new payment app is going. Honestly, it's scary. Papa set it up for me last month with a small amount for emergencies. I didn't feel like I was spending anything. Tap for a samosa. Tap for a cold coffee. Tap for a game character, because it was only a small amount.

Yesterday Papa asked what was left. I checked. Almost nothing. I felt my face burn. With cash, I'd have seen the notes disappearing from my wallet.

Now I've started writing every payment in the back of my diary, with the date. Seeing the list is shocking. But at least I can see it.

Sharmila

qa.q: Where does Sharmila now write every payment?
qa.a: In the back of the diary, with the date.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Papa asked what was left?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed, face burning, on seeing almost nothing remained.

qa.q: Why is writing down each payment a useful habit for Sharmila?
qa.a: Tapping doesn't feel like spending, so a written list brings back the sense of money leaving that cash used to give.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about Sharmila's new diary list?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel reassured that Sharmila is learning to track spending rather than hiding it.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows casual taps on a first payment app feeling like no spending at all, and starting to track payments.

passage: Want to know how I learned about digital money? I'm Madhuri. At fifteen, my parents let me use a payment app for bus fares and lunch. It felt like magic. Scan, tap, done. No coins, no counting. My friend Avni and I would scan for bubble tea, then chips, then little in-game gems. None of it felt real. At the end of the month, my mother showed me the history: over forty payments. I couldn't remember half of them. I was so embarrassed I couldn't look at her. She didn't shout. She just said, "Every Sunday, look at the list with me." That weekly look made the taps feel real again. Now I still check every Sunday, even without her.

qa.q: How many payments did the history show?
qa.a: Over forty payments.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel when the payment history was shown?
qa.a: Madhuri felt deeply embarrassed, unable to look at Mother.

qa.q: Why did the weekly look at the list help?
qa.a: It gave back the sense of money leaving that tapping had removed, turning tracking into a habit.

qa.q: How might Avni have seen their frequent scans?
qa.a: Avni probably saw them as harmless fun at the time, since tapping didn't feel like spending.

grounding: A young person recalls casual taps on a first payment app not feeling like spending, and a weekly check making tracking a habit.

passage:
Monday. Chaitanya, fifteen, got his first UPI access on his mother Zainab's account, with a small monthly limit, for school canteen and bus. By Wednesday he had paid for chips, juice, a phone game upgrade and a friend's birthday treat. It didn't feel like spending. Just tapping.
Friday. The limit ran out. He had no bus fare home and had to call his mother, embarrassed. She came, and on the drive they opened the payment history together. He stared at the list.
The next Monday. Chaitanya made a note on his phone: every payment, every day, with a running total. By Friday he still had some left. "It's weird," he said. "Writing it makes it feel like real money."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya pay for by Wednesday?
qa.a: Chips, juice, a phone game upgrade and a friend's birthday treat.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when he had no bus fare home?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and caught out, having to call his mother.

qa.q: What habit did Chaitanya start, and why did it help?
qa.a: Noting every payment with a running total, which made tapping feel like real money leaving.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel looking at the history with Chaitanya?
qa.a: Zainab might feel concerned but patient, glad to use the drive to help him understand rather than scold.

grounding: Shows over two weeks a teenager whose first UPI taps don't feel like spending, until tracking makes the money feel real.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10, after the cyber-safety session.
Keerthana told the class a story from last week. A stranger messaged her claiming to be from a prize contest: she had won a phone, and he needed her to approve a "collect request" to verify her account. He wrote, "Hurry, the offer ends in ten minutes!" She felt a rush of excitement, then something felt wrong. She didn't approve it, didn't share any code, and showed the message to her mother, who blocked and reported the number. Her friend Binita admitted she had nearly approved a similar request last month. I have added a slide: never share a PIN or OTP, never approve an unexpected request, pause and ask an adult.

qa.q: How long did the stranger say the offer would last?
qa.a: The offer ends in ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when the message arrived?
qa.a: She felt a rush of excitement, then uneasy suspicion that something was wrong.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do right?
qa.a: She didn't approve the request or share any code, and showed the message to her mother, who blocked and reported the number.

qa.q: How might Binita feel hearing Keerthana's story?
qa.a: Binita might feel shaken and relieved, realising she nearly fell for a similar trap.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager pausing on an urgent payment request from a stranger and checking with a parent instead.

passage:
Dear Diary, Thursday.
Weird thing today. Someone messaged me on the gaming app saying they'd give me free game coins if I sent them the OTP that just came to my phone. Then another message: "Quick, it expires in 2 min!" My thumb was literally on the screen. Then I remembered Jasleen didi's rule: "If someone is rushing you about money, stop." So I put the phone down. The OTP message said it was for a payment from our family account.
I showed Jasleen didi. She said I'd just saved Papa's money, and we told Papa together. He called the bank and blocked the number.
I feel a bit shaky still. But proud I stopped.
Jomon

qa.q: How long did the message say the offer would last?
qa.a: It expires in 2 min.

qa.q: How does Jomon feel after stopping?
qa.a: Jomon feels a bit shaky but proud of stopping.

qa.q: What rule helped Jomon, and why does it work?
qa.a: If someone is rushing you about money, stop; scams depend on urgency, so pausing breaks them.

qa.q: How might Jasleen didi feel when Jomon shows the message?
qa.a: Jasleen didi likely felt relieved and proud that the rule worked and Jomon didn't share the OTP.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows refusing to share an OTP under time pressure and checking with family instead.
